Rhaebo blombergi is one of the largest neotropical toads, and its life history reflects a trajectory of substantial investment in somatic growth before reproduction. The maximum recorded body length for females of this species reaches approximately 21 centimeters [Li = approximately 21 centimeters], a size that places them among the most massive bufonids in South America. Males are notably smaller, with an ultimate body length of around 16 centimeters [Li = around 16 centimeters]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is consistent with patterns observed in other large-bodied anurans, where larger female body size is thought to correlate with fecundity advantages. Field surveys and captive records indicate that adult females can achieve an ultimate wet weight of 1135 grams [Wwi = 1135 grams], a value that underscores the sheer biomass this species can attain. In comparison, the wet weight at puberty for females, estimated from relative growth curves similar to those constructed for the common toad Bufo bufo, is approximately 815 grams [Wwp = approximately 815 grams], indicating that reproductive maturity is reached well before maximum size is achieved, leaving substantial room for continued somatic expansion during the adult phase.

Reproductive output in Rhaebo blombergi appears to be concentrated into a single, energetically expensive event each year. Females produce one brood per year [F_R_i = one brood per year] under optimal conditions maintained at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. Within this single annual event, each female lays approximately 82 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 82 eggs per clutch], a number that is modest relative to many smaller bufonid species but likely reflects the considerable investment per offspring. The relatively low fecundity per event may be a consequence of the large egg size, which in turn influences the size of the hatchling. The wet weight at birth for newly emerged larvae is remarkably small, estimated at 0.001 grams [Wwb = 0.001 grams], a value derived from the egg's physical dimensions of approximately 1 millimeter in width and 2 millimeters in length. This tiny starting mass imposes a significant developmental constraint on the early larval period, which must be navigated under specific thermal conditions.

Under laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the embryonic development and subsequent hatching event occur remarkably quickly; the age at birth is approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days]. This abbreviated incubation period is consistent with the pattern seen in many tropical anurans, where elevated temperatures accelerate embryogenesis. Following eclosion, the yolk-sac larva enters a brief endotrophic phase before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The entire period from hatching to the onset of metamorphosis, a critical developmental milestone, spans approximately 141 days  at the same thermal regime at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This relatively extended larval duration is unusual for a tropical bufonid and may reflect the need to accumulate sufficient biomass from a very small birth size before initiating the costly morphological transformation of metamorphic climax.

The metamorphic transition itself represents a substantial physiological bottleneck, after which the terrestrial juvenile faces a prolonged period of growth before reaching sexual functionality. Upon completion of metamorphosis, the recently metamorphosed juvenile has a wet weight of approximately 4.9 grams , representing a nearly five-thousand-fold increase in mass from the 0.001 gram hatchling. This massive gain is achieved through the intensive feeding of the aquatic tadpole stage. The time elapsed since metamorphosis at which individuals attain puberty, marking the onset of gonadal maturation, is estimated at 912 days [tp = 912 days] under conditions of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This period of more than 30 months as a terrestrial juvenile is a substantial fraction of the total lifespan, suggesting that the species prioritizes achieving a large body size—and the associated competitive and fecundity advantages—before committing resources to reproduction. The duration underscores the slow pace of maturation in this giant toad.

Longevity data for Rhaebo blombergi, though limited, suggest a life history strategy oriented toward persistence across multiple breeding seasons. The maximum lifespan recorded under captive conditions at 27 °C [T = 27 °C] is approximately 28.5 years [am = approximately 28.5 years], a remarkable duration for an anuran that aligns with the slow life history pace indicated by its protracted maturation and large body size. This extended lifespan probably buffers the species against years of poor reproductive success, a common evolutionary response in environments with variable resources. The substantial investment in a single, large brood per year, combined with a very long adult life, means that even modest annual fecundity can result in high lifetime reproductive output. The trade-off between early reproduction and continued growth is starkly illustrated by the fact that females can add over 300 grams to their body mass between puberty and their ultimate size, highlighting the selective advantage of delayed reproduction in this colossal amphibian.
